message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be held in a **separate, interest‑bearing account** (unless the landlord is a bank).
• Landlords must provide a written receipt and a statement of the deposit’s location.
• Within **30 days** after you move out, the landlord must return the deposit **minus any lawful deductions** (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection report, and any receipts for repairs.
• Request a written itemization of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a **safe and habitable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Landlords must make repairs within a **reasonable time** after being notified. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or pursue a **repair‑and‑deduct** remedy (pay for repairs yourself and deduct from rent, but only under specific circumstances). | | **Rent Payment & Late Fees** | • The lease sets the rent amount and due date.
• Texas law does **not** limit late fees, but they must be **reasonable** and disclosed in the lease. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble.
• Keep records of all payments. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually **24 hours**) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable” means a time that is convenient for both parties. | • Ask for a written notice of entry and keep a log of visits.
• If you suspect unlawful entry, document the incident. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to **quiet enjoyment** of the premises. Landlords cannot harass or interfere with your privacy. | • Report any harassment or unlawful interference to the landlord or local authorities. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants can terminate with **30 days’ written notice** (or 60 days if the lease is longer).
• Landlords must also give **30 days’ notice** to terminate a month‑to‑month lease. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Texas requires a **written notice** (e.g., 3‑day notice to pay rent or quit, 30‑day notice to vacate for non‑payment, 90‑day notice for lease termination).
• After the notice period, the landlord must file an **eviction lawsuit** (forcible detainer) in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend court hearings and bring all documentation. | | **Rent Control / Rent Increase** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease specifies who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the systems. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord approval. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Resources** | • **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** – consumer protection and housing assistance.
• **Texas Attorney General’s Office** – tenant‑rights guides.
• Local tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union). | • Use these resources for disputes, complaints, or legal representation. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read your lease carefully** – note rent amount, due date, security deposit limits, notice periods, and repair responsibilities. 2. **Document everything** – photos, written notices, receipts, and communication with the landlord. 3. **Keep copies of all payments** – bank statements, checks, or online payment confirmations. 4. **Know your notice requirements** – both for moving out and for the landlord’s right to enter. 5. **Know your rights to habitability** – you can withhold rent or pursue repairs if the landlord fails to maintain the unit. 6. **Seek help early** – if you encounter problems, contact TDHCA, a local tenant‑rights organization, or an attorney before the situation escalates. --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unlawful eviction attempts** (e.g., lock‑out, changing locks without court order). - **Discrimination or harassment** that violates fair‑housing laws. - **Large disputes over security deposits** where the landlord refuses to return the full amount. - **Complex lease terms** that you’re unsure about (e.g., subletting restrictions, pet policies). If you’re facing any of these issues, consider contacting a local attorney who specializes in landlord‑tenant law or a nonprofit legal aid organization.
